permutationLabel: Adolescent with lower abdominal pain and vomiting
summary: 14-year-old boy, sudden right lower abdominal pain and vomiting for 6 h; on examination a high-riding, horizontal, exquisitely tender right testis with absent cremasteric reflex.

inputs.chiefComplaint: Right lower abdominal pain and vomiting
inputs.hpi: Woke at 6 am with sudden pain in the right lower abdomen, vomited twice. Embarrassed; on direct questioning the pain started suddenly in the right testicle and spread to the lower abdomen. No trauma. No urinary symptoms. Onset 6 hours ago.

exam.abdomen: Soft, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding.
exam.other: Genitalia: right testis high-riding with a horizontal lie, exquisitely tender, right hemiscrotum mildly swollen; absent right cremasteric reflex. Left testis normal.

confirmedDiagnosis.name: Right testicular torsion
confirmedDiagnosis.assessmentText: Right testicular torsion (6 hours) — emergency scrotal exploration now, without waiting for imaging; consent for orchidectomy and bilateral fixation.

socratesAnswers.site: Right lower abdomen (RLQ) and right testicle (scrotal)

emergencyLevel.knownGapNote: Web: adaptiveTriage: 'same_day_call' (score 35). No torsion/testicular rule; the scrotal-swelling chip does not raise acuity. iOS: ClinicalPathwayEngine reads only CC/PMH keywords; CC 'Right lower abdominal pain and vomiting' gives 'routine'.
emergencyLevel.proposedFix: Add a triage red flag: male + sudden testicular/scrotal pain (or scrotal-swelling chip) → emergency.

mustExclude.note: Imaging must not delay exploration when torsion is clinically likely.

guideline.name: EAU guidelines on paediatric urology — acute scrotum / testicular torsion
guideline.section: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis; urgent surgical exploration; Doppler only if it does not delay surgery
guideline.citation: Radmayr C, Bogaert G, Burgu B, et al. EAU guidelines on paediatric urology. EAU Guidelines Office, Arnhem, 2024.

rationale: Dangerous mimic of appendicitis in a boy. The genital examination makes the diagnosis; exploration must not wait for imaging.
